verdicts.summary: I tried name collisions across kinds, a driver change on upsert, and usage-limit naming. None of them broke: names are prefixed per kind and include the instance id, driver and field, and the managementKey name with no server host matches the old one. The only hazard the note states, a driver missing from the hand-kept map, is finding 0.

On load, moved field secrets are replaced with the marker and the file is rewritten. A store failure leaves the plaintext in place and the move is retried on the next load, including reloads from the file watcher. Untrusted files are never rewritten.
verdicts.scenario: I tried two cases. (1) The settings file fails to decode: line 840 skips moveInlineSettingsSecrets, so nothing is rewritten. (2) secretStore.set fails for one secret: that name is never added to `moved`, so line 715 keeps its plaintext and the next load retries. I also checked the case where the store already holds an older value for that name: set overwrites it with the file's newer plaintext, which is correct.

verdicts.summary: Every path that sends settings to a client (config load, get, the update response and the change stream) redacts through redactServerSettingsForClient. That function now covers provider config secrets. The web settings code does not read the Antigravity apiKey or the managementKey value anywhere else.
verdicts.scenario: A client saves a new Antigravity apiKey through serverUpdateSettings. The updateSettings result is materialized and holds the plaintext key, but ws.ts:2415 redacts it before the response is sent, so the client only receives the marker.

verdicts.summary: A saved Antigravity API key can no longer be removed from the UI. The settings variant always passes value="", so clearing the field never commits. The provider instance card has no Remove control, unlike SourceControlHostSettings.
verdicts.scenario: 1. A user sets Antigravity authMethod to agent-platform, saves an apiKey, and also fills in gcpProject and gcpLocation. 2. They then want to use the GCP project instead, so they clear the API key field and blur it. 3. useCommitOnBlur sees draft "" equal to value "" and does not commit (the SecretInput guard would also block it). 4. ProviderInstanceCard renders only ProviderSettingsForm for config, with no clear button. 5. The key stays in the secret store and the driver keeps using it, because agent-platform prefers the apiKey over the GCP project. Before this commit the field was a plain DraftInput showing the saved value, and emptying it removed the key (clearWhenEmpty: omit).
verdicts.consequence: Users cannot revoke or remove a saved Antigravity API key, including a leaked one, without deleting the whole provider instance. Agent Platform users cannot switch from the API key to project-based auth.

verdicts.summary: annotateKey merges new annotations into the existing key context, and the default wrapper copies the inner schema's context along. So the flag survives whichever order secretSetting and withDecodingDefault are applied in. Bitbucket's inline settingsSecret: true is also a key annotation.
verdicts.scenario: I tried the Antigravity apiKey, where secretSetting comes before withDecodingDefault and annotateKey(title…) comes after. withDecodingDefault uses decodeTo(self), which only replaces the encoding and keeps self's context (copy at SchemaAST.ts:4259). The later annotateKey spreads the existing context annotations first (SchemaAST.ts:4408), so settingsSecret is kept.

verdicts.summary: No reader of the removed helper or of providerSettingsForm.secret remains anywhere in apps or packages. ProviderSettingsForm is the only file in apps that reads providerSettingsForm, and it now uses isSecretSetting.
verdicts.scenario: I searched the repo for secretSourceControlHostSettingsFields, providerSettingsForm?.secret and annotation.secret. The only hits are vendored alchemy auth-provider fields and the new isSecretSetting mapping. The single former caller now uses secretSettingsFields.
